input:
In this worked example, we are going to look in some detail at how the Hagen-Poiseuille equation can be used to determine the volumetric flow rate of a viscous liquid flowing through a tube under laminar conditions. Let us consider a viscous liquid with a viscosity $\mu$ of 0.05 Pa s, which flows in a laminar manner through a tube having a radius $R$ of 10 mm and a length $L$ of 12 m. When a pressure drop $\Delta P$ of 7 kPa is applied along the tube, the volumetric flow $Q$ turns out to be 164.9 L h-1. The relationship between these quantities is captured by the Hagen-Poiseuille equation, which can be written in the following form:

$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$

It is important to note that this equation rests on a number of important assumptions that should always be borne in mind when it is applied in practice. In particular, the flow is assumed to be laminar, meaning that the liquid moves in smooth layers without mixing across the tube; the flow is assumed to be fully developed, so that the velocity profile no longer changes along the length of the tube; and the liquid is assumed to behave as a Newtonian liquid, with a viscosity that does not depend on how fast it is sheared. It is also worth bearing in mind that the radius appears in the equation raised to the fourth power, which means that the flow is extremely sensitive to the size of the tube, and even a modest change in radius will have a very pronounced effect on the flow that the equation predicts. Where any of these conditions does not hold, the equation should be applied with considerable caution, if at all.
target:
Calculate the volumetric flow of a viscous liquid in laminar flow through a tube, from the following data: viscosity $\mu$ = 0.05 Pa s, tube radius $R$ = 10 mm, tube length $L$ = 12 m, and pressure drop $\Delta P$ = 7 kPa along the tube. The liquid is Newtonian, so its viscosity does not depend on the shear rate. The flow is taken as laminar, with the liquid moving in layers that do not mix across the tube, and as fully developed, with a velocity profile that no longer changes along the tube. The Hagen-Poiseuille equation applies to flow under these conditions and gives the volumetric flow $Q$ as

$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$

where $Q$ is the volumetric flow, $R$ is the tube radius, $\Delta P$ is the pressure drop along the tube, $\mu$ is the viscosity and $L$ is the tube length. In the equation, the pressure drop drives the flow and the viscosity resists it, while the radius enters at the fourth power because a wider tube both presents more area to the flow and allows faster flow at every point of the profile. Substitution of the stated values gives $Q$ = 164.9 L h-1. The fourth power on $R$ makes the radius the quantity to measure with the greatest care: an error in $R$ produces an error in $Q$ about four times as large in proportion, a sensitivity no other input in the equation shares. The result holds only while the flow stays laminar and fully developed and the liquid stays Newtonian; outside those conditions the equation does not apply, and the pressure drop for a given flow rises faster than the equation predicts. Every symbol in the roster is a quantity that can be measured on the tube as installed, which is what makes the equation a calculation from measurements rather than a correlation fitted to them.
